title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Reykjavík: Faster Paths!
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra slice search time by expanding from both start and goal until their frontiers meet. This visualization maps the idea onto real street-grid style graphs like the routes around Reykjavík’s harbor.
ig_caption:
⚡️ Reykjavík streets, but with brains: Bidirectional Dijkstra in action! 🧭

Here’s the core idea (graph nerd edition): instead of running one global Dijkstra from the start, we run two synchronized searches—one forward from the source and one backward from the destination—each using a priority queue and edge weights (like road distance or travel time). ✅ When the two explored regions meet, we can reconstruct the shortest path without expanding every node in the whole graph.

🧩 Graph theory meets real-world maps: treat the street network as a weighted graph where intersections are vertices and road segments are edges. Because we stop early once the “frontiers” overlap, bidirectional search often reduces the explored area compared to a single-direction Dijkstra—especially when the start and goal are not too close to the extremes.

🎥 Want a deeper visualization (frontier growth + meeting point)? Drop a 🔁 and comment “DIJKSTRA” and I’ll generate the next route with different weights (e.g., faster lanes vs scenic streets).
fb_caption:

In a weighted street-map graph, we run Dijkstra from both the start and the goal at the same time. 🎯 As soon as the two searches meet, we stitch together the optimal route—often exploring far fewer intersections than the classic one-way approach.
